sources.news_title: Trump sics his DOJ goons on James Comey—again
sources.text:
It’s equal parts dystopic and pathetic that President Donald Trump can’t stop going after former FBI Director James Comey, the man who arguably helped hand him the 2016 election.
So Trump had his pets at the Department of Justice charge Comey a third time.
Of course, the filing is a nothing burger, telling no one—least of all Comey—much at all about what he did to warrant the charges.
The administration also did something deeply weird, charging Comey by “information” rather than indicting him. The former doesn’t require a grand jury, which is handy for an administration that often gets in trouble for manipulating grand juries and gets no-billed them. But charging by information requires the defendant to waive the right to be indicted, and that won’t happen.
As with all of this administration’s totally fake criminal filings, this is pathetically paltry. Comey is accused of breaking the law by ordering FBI colleagues to leak information to the press on Oct. 5, 2016.
The second count is the exact same thing, except Comey is alleged to have conspired with someone else to leak the materials, ordering “Individual #1 to disclose national defense information to a reporter for a national news publication.”
This is perhaps the weirdest and shoddiest attempt to go after Comey, even more than the seashell case.
First, Comey points out in his motion to dismiss that the charges were filed five years after a generally applicable statute of limitations had expired and five days after the 10-year limit for prosecutions under espionage statutes.
Had the administration indicted Comey rather than charging by information, the 10-year statute of limitations might apply. But since it didn’t, it expired on Oct. 5, 2026.
This has led the DOJ to one of its favorite arguments: You can’t challenge what we’re doing because we haven’t done it yet, even though we’re doing it right now.
So Comey can’t challenge the information filing, which the administration clearly filed to try to stop the 10-year statute of limitations from expiring, creating a placeholder that can hang around indefinitely until it actually indicts him. Instead, the DOJ says Comey has to wait until it indicts him, and then he can challenge it.
DOJ attorneys even had the gall to whine to the court that, because of Comey’s emergency motion, their “efforts on this case were sidelined by efforts to respond to a baseless and unripe motion” and that “undersigned counsel had to draft a response to the emergency motion and appear before this Court.”
How dare the DOJ be required to do its job?
This DOJ hauls people to court under the flimsiest of theories, files emergency motions any time a court case looks like it isn’t going its way, and just generally drags litigants through hell. Whining that Comey’s filing to dismiss is unfair is ridiculous.
Charge first, figure out factual and legal basis later—got it.
Related | Trump team keeps coming up empty in Comey shenanigans
You will not be surprised to learn that the espionage standard relevant here refers only to indictments in the context of the statute of limitations, but the administration’s argument is that, magically, that includes charging by information, and then they can indict him once the statute of limitations runs out.
So what was Comey’s big alleged criminal offense this time around? Somehow being connected to an Oct. 5, 2016, article in The New York Times, in which Comey allegedly told a staff member to speak to reporter Charlie Savage about accuracy concerns. In doing so, per the DOJ, Comey “illegally transferred classified documents.”
Comey’s lawyer, an actually competent attorney and former DOJ special counsel Pat Fitzgerald, noted that the government had already investigated this twice and determined that no charges should be filed.
Of course, Comey has prevailed against the administration on one of its past nonsense theories when he was charged with perjury. That case got thrown out along with interim U.S. Attorney Lindsey Halligan because she was in her role illegally.
Since the statute of limitations ran out on that one, the administration couldn’t recharge him with the same offense. So it ginned up an even more laughable case, charging Comey for posting a picture of some seashells arranged—not even by him!—to spell out “86 47.” The DOJ insisted that this was a clear threat to murder Trump.
Meanwhile, as the DOJ keeps trying to crush Comey, his daughter, Maurene Comey, just won her case over her unlawful termination for the crime of having the same last name as her dad. The court ordered the DOJ to reinstate her with back pay.
The judge in that case didn’t buy that Trump has the power to reach down and fire career attorneys, even if they share the same last name with someone he’s fixated on.
In doing so, he declined to adopt Trump’s sweeping “new and expansive theory of executive power.” Allowing that would essentially eradicate the civil service protection that people in Comey’s role can only be fired for cause.
Of course, the administration has already said it’s appealing Maurene Comey’s reinstatement. And it will certainly run to the Supreme Court to whine about it. And why not? The court’s conservatives love giving Trump more power as much as they love screwing federal workers, so this is right up their alley.

sources.news_title: The Justice Department's 3rd attempt to imprison James Comey stinks of Trump's desperation for revenge
sources.text:
The Justice Department's 3rd Attempt To Imprison James Comey Stinks of Trump's Desperation for Revenge
Prosecutors allege that the former FBI director illegally disclosed classified information in 2016—an incident that was investigated twice without resulting in charges.
A little more than a year ago, President Donald Trump publicly demanded that Pam Bondi, then the attorney general, find a crime to pin on former FBI Director James Comey. Trump's underlings have repeatedly tried to do that, first charging Comey with lying to Congress and then accusing him of threatening to assassinate the president. But the first indictment was dismissed because Trump had illegally appointed the prosecutor who obtained it, and the second was doomed right out of the gate because it aimed to punish constitutionally protected political speech.
The Justice Department's latest attempt to follow Trump's marching orders was revealed on Monday, when U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden unsealed a "criminal information" that claims Comey illegally shared classified information with The New York Times on October 5, 2016. In an attempt to meet the statutory deadline for that charge, prosecutors filed it exactly 10 years after the alleged disclosure. But Comey's lawyers argue that federal law required the government to obtain a grand jury indictment within 10 years of the alleged offense, which it failed to do.
Whatever you make of that dispute, the president has made it clear that he wants to imprison Comey, a longtime nemesis because of his role in the "Russiagate hoax" during Trump's first term, and does not much care about exactly how that happens. Justice Department officials, meanwhile, are keen to pursue Trump's personal vendetta by using their prosecutorial powers as an instrument of his revenge.
The new case "would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice," Comey said in an online video on Monday. "I'm still innocent. I'm still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary."
In the New York Times story at the center of the case, Charlie Savage and Nicole Perloth reported that Yahoo had adapted "a system intended to scan emails for child pornography" to comply with a Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court order seeking "messages containing a computer 'signature' tied to the communications of a state-sponsored terrorist organization." Savage and Perloth cited "two government officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity."
Dustin Farahnak, a special U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, says that story included "first-time disclosures of classified information not intended for the public domain." According to Farahnak, the government has evidence that Comey "directed staff" to discuss "specific accuracy concerns" about a prior Reuters report on the same subject with Savage. In the process of doing that, Farahnak says, those FBI officials "illegally transferred classified information."
Comey's attempt to set the record straight, according to Trump's henchmen, was a felony punishable by up to 10 years in prison under 18 USC 793(d), an Espionage Act provision that applies to an official who "willfully" shares "information relating to the national defense" with an unauthorized recipient when he "has reason to believe" it "could be used to the injury of the United States." Comey also faces a charge of conspiring to violate Section 793, which likewise carries a maximum 10-year sentence.
If Comey's alleged disclosure was such a grave crime, you might wonder, why did it take a decade to charge him? Because two prior investigations of the same incident concluded that criminal charges were not warranted.
Beginning in March 2017, John Durham, the U.S. attorney for the District of Connecticut, looked into the genesis of the Times article. The investigation found that James Baker, then the FBI's general counsel, was one of the anonymous sources. Baker said he had acted under instructions from FBI Chief of Staff James Rybacki, whom he understood to be conveying Comey's wishes. Durham's investigation included interviews, emails, phone records, and consideration of the relevant statutes. In December 2018, Comey's lawyers note, Durham "wrote a classified memorandum outlining the investigation and recommending 'NO prosecution for Baker or anyone else.'"
The following month, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia "opened an investigation into the same subject matter," Comey's lawyers say. That investigation "was closed without any charges in February 2020" after the office "declined to prosecute."
Given the outcomes of those two investigations, the decision to charge Comey now stinks of desperation to slake Trump's thirst for revenge. According to Comey's lawyers, the tardiness of the charges also fatally undermines the case.
Federal law generally requires that prosecutors file charges within five years of the alleged crime. But the Internal Security Act of 1950 made an exception for Section 793, saying "an indictment for any violation" of that provision "may be found at any time within ten years next after such violation shall have been committed."
The charges against Comey "should be dismissed as time barred," his lawyers argue: "Section 19 of the Internal Security Act gives the government an extended ten-year limitations period in which to charge Section 793 offenses. But as Section 19 unambiguously states, the government may invoke that extended period only by obtaining a grand jury indictment. A criminal information—which the government can issue unilaterally without grand jury involvement—does not suffice. Because the default five-year statute of limitations for federal felonies has long since elapsed on the alleged offenses, and the government's information does not meet the express statutory requirement for an extended ten-year limitations period, the information is untimely and must be dismissed."
Whichever side prevails on that issue, no one should have any illusions that the Justice Department is pursuing the mission suggested by its name. "It remains unclear what [McFadden] will do with the matter and whether DOJ will even be able to secure an indictment—as required by the Constitution," Cato Institute legal fellow Mike Fox says in an emailed press release. "Should the matter proceed, it is unequivocally clear that this case is a vindictive prosecution—a classic case of lawfare by a weaponized Justice Department."

sources.news_title: Former FBI Director James Comey is charged with 2 federal crimes in Washington, D.C. It is his third case in a year: 'Well, they’re back again'
sources.text:
A criminal information filed on Oct. 5 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia charges former FBI Director James Comey with two federal offenses. According to Mediaite, the charges concern the alleged unauthorized sharing of national defense information with a reporter. This is the third criminal case brought against him in about one year.
Prosecutors say Comey violated the Espionage Act by unlawfully transmitting national defense information to someone who was not authorized to receive it. A separate count accuses him of conspiracy to commit that same offense. The three-page filing does not name the reporter, the news outlet, any co-conspirators, or the specific information that was allegedly shared.
According to the prosecutors, Comey acted through one or more co-conspirators on Oct. 5, 2016, and directed a person labeled only as “Individual #1” to give national defense information to a reporter at a national news publication. The alleged conspiracy began no later than Oct. 4, 2016, and continued up to the day the information was filed.
Comey posts video response while attorney outlines prior cases and current defense
Comey answered the charges in a 35-second video he posted on Substack. “Well, they’re back again,” he said. “It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice – one that we cannot become numb to. Nothing’s changed with me. I’m still innocent. I’m still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary,” he continued.
“And I’m still lucky to have an amazing family and an incredible group of lawyers that will stand up in court and fight the latest, and whatever comes after this,” Comey concluded.
Under the Trump administration, Comey has already faced other criminal cases. One earlier indictment accused him of making false statements to Congress and obstructing a congressional proceeding; those charges were later dismissed. In a different case, he was charged with two felonies over a social media post that showed seashells arranged to form the numbers “86 47,” which was seen as a threat against Trump’s life by the prosecutors.
Even though the administration has suffered setbacks in its earlier attempts to prosecute Comey, it has continued to pursue legal action against the former FBI chief. The newest filing arrives after the Justice Department reportedly opened an investigation in late August into claims that Comey leaked classified information to the media. As part of that probe, a subpoena was issued to his former adviser, Daniel Richman.
Richman had previously said he shared the contents of one of Comey’s memos with The New York Times. The court document itself does not say whether the current charges grew out of that investigation.
Comey’s lawyer, Pat Fitzgerald, released a statement that CNN’s Kaitlan Collins posted on X. Fitzgerald said, “For the third time in little more than one year, the Department of Justice has attempted to charge Mr. Comey with a federal crime. Mr. Comey steadfastly maintains his innocence.”
He described the September 2025 case by saying the Department of Justice “used a person who was not actually a United States Attorney to seek an Indictment that was not actually shown to the grand jury. And it charged Mr. Comey with crimes that he did not commit. That case was promptly and properly dismissed.”
Fitzgerald also addressed the April 2026 charges filed in the Eastern District of North Carolina. Those involved “Mr. Comey’s posting of a photograph of seashells spelling ‘8647.’” He added, “We will not comment beyond our filings in that case.”
On the present matter, Fitzgerald said it concerns an October 5, 2016 New York Times article that two separate teams of prosecutors looked into during the first Trump administration. Both times, “the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone.”
He continued that, ten years after the article appeared, the government filed an “Information” against Comey “that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury. It purports to charge Mr. Comey with crimes that he did not commit.”
Politico reported that the New York Times story described how Yahoo changed its spam filter to handle FBI surveillance requests. Prosecutors claim Comey allowed then-FBI General Counsel James Baker to leak classified material to the newspaper.
Comey’s attorneys maintain that the statute of limitations ran out on Oct. 5 and that the Justice Department tried improperly to get around the 10-year limit that applies to certain national security offenses. Fitzgerald closed the statement by saying, “We are gratified that United States District Judge Trevor McFadden has ordered this matter unsealed. Mr. Comey will fight these charges vigorously and in the open.”

sources.news_title: Former FBI Director James Comey Responds as Trump's DOJ Unseals a Third Criminal Case Against Him: 'Nothing's Changed With Me, I'm Still Innocent'
sources.text:
'Nothing's Changed With Me, I'm Still Innocent': James Comey Responds as Trump's DOJ Unseals a Third Criminal Case Against Him
Oct. 27 2026, Published 11:40 a.m. ET
President Donald Trump's Department of Justice is still going after former FBI director James Comey.
Comey was charged on Monday, October 27, 2026, in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., marking a third attempt to put him behind bars by the Trump administration.
However, Comey continues to insist he's totally innocent, RadarOnline.com has learned.
James Comey Denies Allegations in Third Federal Indictment
Addressing supporters, he said in a video: "Nothing's changed with me. I'm still innocent."
Further, he slammed the incessant attempts to jail him as an "appalling abuse of the Department of Justice," urging the public to avoid becoming "numb" to Trump's tactics.
Comey added: "And I’m still lucky to have an amazing family and an incredible group of lawyers that will stand up in court and fight the latest and whatever comes after this.
"The next couple of years are going to be hard for all of us. It's really important that we stand straight and keep the faith in America."
Comey Accused of Leaking Sensitive Information
In the latest case, Comey was charged with knowingly communicating information related to national defense to a person not entitled to receive it and conspiring with others to violate the law against sharing such information.
The latest indictment alleged he worked with at least one other person "to disclose national defense information to a reporter for a national news publication."
They pointed to an alleged conversation in October 2016 between Comey and The New York Times, during which prosecutors claimed he breached protocol with the "disclosure of classified information."
In response, Comey's attorneys sought to dismiss the case, arguing the statute of limitations on the alleged crime expired.
Patrick Fitzgerald, his attorney, responded: "For the third time in little more than one year, the Department of Justice has attempted to charge Mr. Comey with a federal crime. Mr. Comey steadfastly maintains his innocence."
Previous Indictments Challenged
Comey was formerly indicted on two other charges.
In North Carolina, Comey was charged with threatening Trump's life via a post shared on social media.
In a photo posted by Comey, seashells were outlined on the beach to read "86 47."
Prosecutors alleged the numbers were a call to kill Trump, as "86" is code in restaurants to indicate a menu item is no longer available.
Comey denied the alleged intent behind the photo. His attorneys are seeking to have the indictment tossed out of court.
Additionally, Comey was charged with allegedly falsely testifying to Congress. Prosecutors alleged he lied to Congress when he allegedly falsely denied authorizing another FBI employee to plant an anonymous source in news reports.
Particularly, the alleged news leaks centered around an investigation of Hillary Clinton and her emails during the 2016 presidential election.
However, the case was dismissed after the judge determined Lindsey Halligan, a stand-in U.S. attorney prosecuting the case, was invalidly appointed, rendering the indictment irrelevant.
President Obama Backs Comey
The repetitive cases against Comey have repeatedly been denied. Plus, he's received an outpouring of support from Trump adversaries, including former President Barack Obama, who spoke out before the third indictment hit.
The former president likened recent attacks against Representative Ilhan Omar as similar to Comey.
He wrote on X: "It is a basic principle of American democracy that the government can't selectively target individuals simply because of their political beliefs or what they say. But that's exactly what the Trump Administration is doing to Congresswoman Ilhan Omar of Minnesota."
"It's not the first time this has happened," the 65-year-old noted, citing the DOJ's attempt to prosecute Comey and members of the Federal Reserve.

DOJ Brings Third Criminal Case Against Former FBI Director James Comey Over Alleged Classified Information Leak
by Emmitt Barry, Worthy News Washington D.C. Bureau Chief
(Worthy News) – The Justice Department has launched a third criminal case against former FBI Director James Comey, accusing him of illegally disclosing classified national security information to a journalist in 2016, according to federal court documents unsealed Monday.
Prosecutors allege that Comey directed FBI personnel to provide sensitive information to a New York Times reporter concerning a secret surveillance program involving Yahoo and U.S. intelligence agencies.
The filing accuses Comey of transmitting national defense information and conspiring to transmit such information. Unlike a grand jury indictment, however, the charges were filed through a legal document known as a criminal information, leaving prosecutors with additional procedural hurdles before a trial can proceed.
The Justice Department filed the document under seal on October 5, seeking to preserve the case before the expiration of a 10-year statute of limitations.
Comey’s attorneys have challenged the prosecution, arguing that the government failed to obtain a timely grand jury indictment. Federal prosecutors maintain that their filing legally preserved the charges.
Third Prosecution Under Trump Administration
The latest case follows two previous criminal proceedings against Comey since President Donald Trump returned to the White House.
The first, involving allegations that Comey lied to Congress about media disclosures, was dismissed after a federal judge determined that the prosecutor who brought the case had been improperly appointed.
A second case, involving allegations that Comey threatened Trump through a social media post featuring seashells arranged to read “8647,” remains pending.
The newest allegations were previously examined by federal investigators during Trump’s first administration. According to Comey’s defense attorneys, both investigations ended without criminal charges.
Comey, whom Trump dismissed in May 2017 amid the FBI’s investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election, continues to deny wrongdoing.
“I’m still innocent,” Comey said in a video statement Monday, accusing the Justice Department of abusing its authority.
His attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, said the former FBI director would vigorously contest the allegations.

The charges that were filed are a criminal information, which is a charge filed by prosecutors, not a grand jury indictment. In the filing, the Justice Department said the move is to buy time before the statute of limitations expires.
“The Department filed a waiverless criminal information to toll the statute of limitations as it relates to allegations concerning former FBI Director Comey,” prosecutors wrote, adding that the case is “an ongoing criminal investigation.”
In an Oct. 20 filing, Mr. Comey’s attorneys moved to dismiss the case, arguing that an indictment must be filed within 10 years and that a criminal information does not suffice. They said the case is “time-barred” because the government did not obtain a grand jury indictment after Oct. 5, 2016, when the alleged crime occurred.
“An indictment fundamentally differs from an information,” his attorneys wrote.
The new charges arise from an Oct. 5, 2016, article in The New York Times that blared the headline, “Yahoo Said to Have Aided U.S. Email Surveillance by Adapting Spam Filter,” written by reporters Charlie Savage and Nicole Perlroth.
“The United States’ investigation has uncovered evidence that former FBI Director, James B. Comey, sought to correct misinformation which had appeared in the press by way of Reuters the day before,” Special Assistant U.S. Attorney Dustin Farahnak wrote in the filing unsealed Monday.
“The investigation has uncovered evidence that Mr. Comey directed staff to speak to Mr. Savage about specific accuracy concerns related to the Reuters article, and thereby illegally transferred classified information.”
Mr. Comey was the FBI director when the Times article was published.
Mr. Trump has repeatedly called for Mr. Comey to be prosecuted, referring to him as “a dirty cop” and a “sick person.” The former FBI director launched an investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election and into alleged links between Russia and the Trump campaign.
Since Mr. Trump returned to the White House, Mr. Comey has been charged three times in federal criminal cases.
The first case, filed in Virginia, charged Mr. Comey with making false statements and obstructing a congressional procedure during his September 2020 testimony before the Senate Judiciary Committee regarding anonymous press sourcing. A federal judge dismissed the indictment after ruling that the interim U.S. attorney who filed the charges was unlawfully appointed. The Justice Department has appealed.
The second case, filed in North Carolina, accused Mr. Comey of making a threat via a social media post featuring a photo of seashells arranged to spell “86 47,” which the Justice Department said was an assassination threat against Mr. Trump, because he is the 47th president and “86” is sometimes a slang term meaning “to get rid of.”
Mr. Comey has maintained his innocence in that case, which is still ongoing.
Patrick Fitzgerald, Mr. Comey’s attorney, said the most recent charges involve two different teams of prosecutors that investigated the allegations during the first Trump administration.
“Both times, the government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone. Now 10 years after the article was published, the government filed an ’information’ against Mr. Comey that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury and ’purports to charge Mr. Comey with a crime that he did not commit.’
“Mr. Comey will fight these charges vigorously and in the open,” Mr. Fitzgerald said.
This article was made available to WMAL via The Washington Times.

THE DAILY BS: HOW MUCH CAN YOU HANDLE?
SPARE ME THE BS (I’ve got things to do).
- Prosecutors filed a criminal information alleging former FBI Director James Comey improperly disclosed sensitive national defense information in 2016.
- The latest filing does not include a grand-jury indictment, raising procedural and limitations questions.
- The same day, a federal judge ruled that Comey’s daughter Maurene had been unlawfully fired by the Justice Department.
LAY IT ON ME (I’ve got time).
James Comey has another appointment with the federal justice system. And this time, the Justice Department has produced something unusual: a criminal charging document without a grand-jury indictment.
For a former FBI director who spent years explaining proper legal procedure to the rest of America, the procedural details are becoming quite a story of their own.
Federal prosecutors filed a two-count criminal information accusing Comey of transmitting national defense information to an unauthorized recipient. It concerns alleged disclosures in October 2016 while Comey was running the FBI.
According to prosecutors, Comey directed staff members to communicate sensitive information concerning American email surveillance to a New York Times reporter. Comey denies the allegations.
Here’s where the prosecution takes an especially interesting turn: prosecutors did not secure an indictment. Instead, they filed a criminal information, ordinarily used in felony cases when a defendant waives indictment.
Comey has shown no inclination to cooperate with the government’s allegations. A Justice Department spokesperson told CBS News the filing was intended to preserve the case before the statute of limitations expired.
That’s a notable explanation: prosecutors are pursuing allegations dating back a decade while navigating a legal deadline. Comey’s lawyers dispute the case, including its procedural footing.
The filing was originally sealed and became public Monday at Comey’s request. He responded: “It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice.” He also insisted, “Nothing’s changed with me. I’m still innocent.”
Meanwhile, his daughter Maurene Comey won a separate ruling that her dismissal as a Manhattan federal prosecutor was unlawful.
So in one federal courtroom James Comey was confronting new allegations from the Trump DOJ, and in another his daughter was winning a legal dispute against that department. Try selling that plot to a television producer; he’ll tell you the script is getting complicated.
The two legal disputes are separate. The new criminal information does not resolve whether the case can proceed or whether Comey committed any offense.
But the legal fight between Trump-era prosecutors and the former FBI director remains far from finished, with procedure now nearly as important as the underlying allegations.

Trump DOJ Charges James Comey a Third Time Over Alleged Leaks
The latest charges came just hours after a federal judge ruled that the Department of Justice had illegally fired Comey’s daughter.
Former FBI Director James Comey
Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images
Former FBI Director James Comey
The Trump administration has just charged James Comey for a third time.
The Department of Justice alleged that the former FBI director leaked national defense information 10 years ago, according to court filings made public Monday. The DOJ claims that Comey was the source of national security information that ended up in a 2016 New York Times report.
Prosecutors filed a “waiverless criminal information” in Washington, D.C., federal court, allowing them to bring charges without an indictment and extend the 10-year statute of limitations to get one. Comey vowed to fight any charges in a video he posted Monday.
“It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to. Nothing’s changed with me, I’m still innocent, I’m still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary,” Comey said, adding that prosecutors waited too long to bring the charges.
Comey: "Well, they're back again.
It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice. One that we cannot become numb to.
Nothing's changed with me. I'm still innocent. I'm still not afraid of these people. And I still believe in the independent federal judiciary.
And I'm still lucky to have an amazing family and an incredible group of lawyers and will stand up in court and fight the latest. And whatever comes after this, the next couple of years are going to be hard for all of us.
It's really important that we stand straight and keep the faith in America."
President Donald Trump still holds a grudge against Comey over the FBI’s investigation into ties between Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign and Russia. He fired Comey in 2017, and in Trump’s second term, the DOJ tried to indict the former director for allegedly lying in a 2020 congressional hearing, only for that case to fall apart because the prosecutor was improperly appointed.
Later, federal prosecutors charged Comey for somehow trying to threaten the president’s life with a social media post of seashells on a beach spelling out “86 47.” The government argued that Comey used “86,” a slang term meaning “get rid of,” to say “kill” and used “47” to mean Trump, the forty-seventh president of the U.S. That case remains pending.
The new charges came just hours after a judge ruled that Comey’s daughter Maurene, the former assistant U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, was wrongfully terminated in July 2025, and ordered the DOJ to reinstate her with back pay. No reason was given for her dismissal, although her last name may have been a factor.
Ohio Venues Keep Canceling on Vivek Ramasamy After That Campaign Ad
The Republican nominee for governor is having trouble finding venues for his campaign events after defending his advertisement with Amy Acton’s mother.
Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy joins other Republicans at a rally at the annual Circleville Pumpkin Show, on October 23.
Spencer Platt/Getty Images
Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy joins other Republicans at a rally at the annual Circleville Pumpkin Show, on October 23.
Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy is struggling to book venues in his home state just days before the midterms, amid growing backlash to his unreasonably cruel attack ad against Democratic opponent Amy Acton.
Two Ohio restaurants—Elliot’s Wood Fired Kitchen and The Old Dog Ale House & Brewery—have canceled events with the Ohio Republican Party featuring Ramaswamy after he released and then doubled down on his advert featuring Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur. An event the party was supposed to host on Tuesday now lists “to be announced” as the location.
The ad features Arthur accusing her daughter of lying about how she was raised. But Arthur lost custody of Acton after her husband, Cledith “Bud” Arthur, was arrested for raping Acton when she was just 12 years old. Bud skipped bail and left town with Acton’s mother, who stayed married to him until his death. Now she is being platformed by Ramaswamy, calling her daughter who survived years of sexual abuse a liar on camera.
That cruelty is negatively impacting Ramaswamy’s campaign. An anonymous Ohio Republican even told Zeteo that they were “getting calls that people don’t want him there.” Other venues that hosted Ramaswamy over the weekend have been flooded by one-star reviews on Google.
Aside from the restaurants, Ramaswamy has been rebuked by every living governor of Ohio, Democrat and Republican, for the ad—which has continued to run. Former Republican Governor Mike DeWine said that it was “wrong” to run the ad last week and urged the Ramaswamy campaign to take it down.
Even still, Ramaswamy, President Trump, and Vice President JD Vance have continued to defend the decision to run the ad, while Acton’s brother Philip Stearns lambasted the campaign last week.
“It’s not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother’s husband into a political talking point,” Stearnssaid. “After he was arrested and Amy and I were removed from their custody, our birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died. This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core—a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants.”
Major Ohio Paper Breaks Own Rule on Endorsements to Trash Ramaswamy
The nearly two-century-old Cleveland Plain Dealer broke with precedent to endorse Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton.
Michael Swensen/Getty Images
Vivek Ramaswamy’s dirty political schemes are making history.
The Ohio Republican gubernatorial nominee’s boorish ad campaign against Democratic candidate Dr. Amy Acton has inspired one of Ohio’s oldest newspapers, Cleveland’s The Plain Dealer, to break company policy in Acton’s favor.
The paper had stated a few months ago it would not make political endorsements, including in the governor’s race. But on Sunday, its editorial board published a statement declaring it stood firmly behind Acton.
The weekly’s decision is just the latest in a tsunami of public backlash against Ramaswamy and his team after they aired an advertisement earlier this month that featured Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur. In the ad, Arthur claimed that “Amy has a serious problem.”
The MAGA Republicans arranged the cameo despite the fact that Acton had not spoken to her mother since she was 12 years old, and that Arthur abandoned her two children to skip town with her husband, who was indicted for allegedly raping Acton when she was a young girl.
“A candidate who uses childhood sexual abuse as a weapon against the person who endured it has crossed a line that Ohioans should defend, whatever their party,” the newspaper’s editorial board wrote.
“We are better than this. We have a responsibility to show it,” it continued. “We made our endorsement policy to serve our readers. We cannot let it become a reason to remain silent when we believe Ohio faces a choice this consequential.”
Dozens of Republicans—including Ohio Governor Mike DeWine—have since come out against Ramaswamy’s tasteless ad, advising the former Trump official to take it down.
Nonetheless, Ramaswamy has repeatedly defended the ad. On Friday, he told the Ohio Capital Journal that the message had “nothing to do with childhood abuse, sexual abuse.”
“Our ad was about a consistent track record of Amy Acton telling lies, including during this campaign,” Ramaswamy said.
But the voting public has not seen it that way. Protesters have begun to appear outside of Ramaswamy’s speaking engagements. At a campaign event in Strongsville last week, demonstrators held up signs that likened Ramaswamy to a snake: “Nobody slithers lower than Vivek #VileAds,” read one posterboard recorded by the Journal. Others said Ramaswamy “defends child predators,” protects “pedos,” and “exploits child abuse for votes.”
The negative rhetoric has begun to materialize in damaging ways for the biotech billionaire. Several Ohio venues canceled Ramaswamy’s speaking events over the weekend, apparently concerned about the fallout should they be affiliated with his drowning reputation.
Woman Says Trump Raped Her and Then Said “The Show Must Go On”
House Democrats have released a 50-page report on the Epstein files cover-up—and it reveals a new rape allegation against Donald Trump.
Jeffrey Epstein and Donald Trump pose together at the Mar-a-Lago estate, Palm Beach, Florida, February 22, 1997.
Davidoff Studios/Getty Images
Jeffrey Epstein and Donald Trump pose together at the Mar-a-Lago estate, Palm Beach, Florida, February 22, 1997.
A new rape allegation has been leveled against President Trump in a report released by House Democrats Monday detailing the White House’s cover-up of the Jeffrey Epstein files.
Beatrice Keul, a model and former Miss Switzerland, told Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee that Trump violently raped her in a hotel room at his Plaza Hotel in New York in 1993, when she was 24 years old.
According to the Democrats’ report, Keul said Trump grabbed her from behind and raped her, which she described as “brutal.” He allegedly tore her dress, bruised her in multiple places, and caused her to bleed. Afterward, she said he sat her on the edge of the bed, repeated promises he had made earlier that his associate, modeling agent Paolo Zampolli, would help her with a U.S. visa and admission to New York University, and made her promise to keep quiet. (Zampolli would later hold roles in both Trump administrations.)
“The show must go on,” Trump allegedly told her. Months later, he reached out to her and again promised to help her get a visa and go to NYU, but she declined assistance, according to the report.
Previously, the Swiss model told the Daily Mailin 2024 that Trump only attempted to assault her, jumping on top of her and groping her. In that account, she said he backed off after she resisted.
“I tried everything I could. Finally, I said, ‘Let’s talk first’ or something like that, then he slowed down,” Keul said in that interview. The Democrats’ report does not mention why Keul decided to change her story.
The report states that the assault happened while Keul was in the U.S. for Trump’s American Dream Pageant for 16- to 22-year-olds, and that he introduced himself to her at a press luncheon for the event, where she also met Epstein. The billionaire financier introduced himself as “Jeffrey, Don’s best friend,” spending 10 minutes talking to her while grinning sideways at Trump, who was watching them talk from afar, according to the report.
Keul alleges that Epstein also made promises to her, saying, “You know I can take care of you. We organize many parties with Don.”
“Flights, accommodations, you don’t have to worry about anything,” Epstein said per the report.
The report states that Trump’s promise of NYU admission is part of a pattern of Epstein promising an NYU education to “lure in and then control his victims,” and that Keul would have no way of knowing this when she mentioned Trump’s offer to the Daily Mail in 2024, months before Epstein’s NYU offers were revealed in later public reports.
The incident also fits with Epstein’s usual practices, as he often called foreign pageant winners and invited them to visit him in Florida, according to the report. An unnamed assistant to Epstein in the 1990s has reportedly said that “on dozens of occasions in the mid-1990s, the financier instructed her to call a pageant winner from somewhere in the world and invite her to visit him in Florida.”
The White House has denied the allegations, with spokesperson Lauren Bis telling HuffPost in an email, “This ‘report’ is nothing more than a desperate attempt by crazed Democrats to distract Americans from the surging Republican momentum driven by President Trump’s historic achievements. The President kicked Jeffrey Epstein out of his club at Mar-a-Lago because he was a creep, and he has been fully exonerated of anything related to Epstein.”
No Wonder Trump Doesn’t Care About Gas Prices. It’s Making Him Rich.
Donald Trump’s personal holdings in the oil and gas industry have ballooned in value.
Brendan SMIALOWSKI/AFP/Getty Images
It’s no surprise that President Donald Trump thinks that the oil and gas business is more important than lowering gas prices: He’s the one making a fortune.
A new report published Monday by the Democrats on the Congressional Joint Economic Committee revealed that the value of Trump’s personal holdings in oil and gas may have increased by 43 percent in the last 10 months alone.
The president’s oil and gas holdings are currently worth between $22.5 million and $81.6 million. At the end of 2025, they were worth between $12.6 million and $46 million.
The report came out shortly after the president started bragging about how the energy prices hurting Americans are making him and his billionaire buddies rich.
“And while oil prices are temporarily high, and will be falling dramatically in a short period of time as soon as that war is over—because there’s so much oil,” he said to the crowd at a rally in Georgia on Saturday, referring to his war in Iran.
“The United States oil and gas business is making hundreds of billions of dollars.… Our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars ’cause of what’s happened in the Middle East … trillions of dollars.”
Meanwhile, the average price Americans are paying for gasoline under Trump has officially surpassed the average price during the Biden administration. Trump has repeatedly pledged to end his seven-month “six-week war” with Iran and lower gasoline prices to below $2 per gallon. But what reason does he have to end the war and lower prices when he’s openly admitting it’s in his financial interest to let Americans suffer? And what kind of message does this send to Americans ahead of the midterm elections, where Trump wants voters to pretend his name is on the ballot?

sources.news_title: Justice Department Files More Charges Against James Comey
sources.text:
The Justice Department has brought charges against former FBI Director James Comey for the third time in 13 months, this time related to alleged leaks of national security information to the media.
According to court documents filed earlier this month and unsealed on Monday, federal prosecutors are accusing Comey of “willfully” mishandling information related to national defense in October 2016, resulting in the information appearing in media reports.
“Having reason to believe such information could be used to injure the United States and to the advantage of any foreign nation,” the court document said Comey “knowingly and willfully communicated, delivered, transmitted, and caused that information to be communicated, delivered, and transmitted to a person not entitled to receive it.”
The inquiry is the latest attempt to prosecute Comey, who is a prominent critic of President Donald Trump. Trump fired Comey in 2017 while Comey was leading the FBI investigation into potential ties between Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign and Russia. The first Trump Administration cited a memo related to Comey’s handling of the FBI investigation into Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton’s emails. Since then, Trump has publicly called for criminal investigations into Comey and celebrated the indictments he’s faced.
In a video posted on Monday, Comey said the latest investigation was an attempt to politically persecute him.
“They’re back, again,” Comey said. “It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to.”
“I’m still innocent. I’m still not afraid of these people,” he added.
Comey’s attorneys argued in court filings that the alleged leaks had already been investigated twice during the first Trump Administration in 2017 and 2019, and neither had resulted in charges.
The Justice Department has pursued a number of investigations and indictments against prominent Democrats in recent weeks, appearing to break with the unofficial “unwritten 60-day rule” of avoiding filing new charges or taking public investigatory action that could influence an approaching election. Earlier this month, the Department secured a search warrant for the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D, Minn.), who called the effort “the latest escalation in [Trump’s] campaign of political intimidation.” The DOJ also secured an indictment against Virginia Senate Leader Louise Lucas, who led the Democrats’ counter-effort against Republican gerrymandering, on drug trafficking and money laundering charges. Lucas denied the allegations and said she would fight back against an attempt by “people in power … to silence those who stand up to them.”
What to know about the new Comey charges
According to court documents, prosecutors allege that around Oct. 4 and 5, 2016, Comey directed FBI staff to speak with the New York Times “about specific accuracy concerns” related to “misinformation which had appeared” in a Reuters report about Yahoo’s cooperation with U.S. surveillance.
In doing so, prosecutors contend, Comey “illegally transferred classified information.”
The Times article had described how Yahoo had adapted its existing email filtering system, used to detect spam, malware, and child sexual abuse material, to comply with a secret surveillance order to search messages for a computer “signature” associated with communications by a foreign, state-sponsored terrorist organization. The article said the Justice Department had obtained the order from a Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court judge in 2015 and that Yahoo was barred from disclosing it.
A spokesperson for the Times said the newspaper “does not comment on the sourcing behind our reporting, but we know from experience that prosecutions like this one are designed to discourage sources from providing journalists with the kind of valuable and illuminating information that the public needs to know.”
Comey’s lawyers argued in a motion to dismiss the case that the Trump Administration did not file an indictment within the 10-year statute of limitations. On Oct. 5, prosecutors filed the charges in a criminal information under seal in Federal District Court in Washington, which does not require approval from a grand jury or a judicial finding of probable cause, but have not obtained an indictment.
Previous charges against Comey
The Justice Department has brought multiple charges against Comey during Trump’s second term. It secured an indictment against him in September 2025 over allegations that he made false statements to Congress in 2020 related to alleged leaks to the media. The charges were thrown out by a federal judge in November, concluding that the prosecutor, Lindsey Halligan, had been unlawfully appointed.
Comey was also indicted in April over allegedly making a threat against Trump by posting on Instagram a photograph of seashells on a North Carolina beach arranged to spell “86 47.” Prosecutors argued that the arrangement was intended as a threat “to kill” Trump, who is the 47th President. Comey, who deleted the post after initial backlash, said he did not intend the photograph to be a threat against Trump, and that he understood the numbers to be a “political message.” The numbers “86” have commonly been used to mean “to throw out” or “to refuse service to,” according to Merriam-Webster, but have also been used in some instances to mean “to kill.”
That case is set to go to trial in North Carolina in February 2027.
Earlier on Monday, a federal judge in New York ruled that the Justice Department had unlawfully fired Comey’s daughter, Maurene Comey, in July 2025. The judge ordered her retroactive reinstatement with back pay, concluding that the Trump Administration had violated the Constitution and federal law by claiming the President had executive authority to fire civil servants.

By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
The Justice Department has initiated a third criminal case against former FBI Director James Comey, accusing him of unlawfully disclosing national defense information to a journalist in October 2016 and conspiring with others to facilitate the alleged disclosure.
The two-count criminal information, filed Oct. 5 in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia and unsealed Monday, Oct. 26, alleges that Comey directed the transmission of sensitive government information to a reporter while serving as FBI director.
According to Fox News’ reporting on the newly disclosed charges, prosecutors accuse Comey of knowingly and willfully communicating information related to national defense to someone unauthorized to receive it.
The allegations involve communications with a New York Times journalist concerning U.S. email surveillance operations in October 2016. Prosecutors contend that Comey directed others to disclose information connected to a news report about government surveillance activities.
The criminal information alleges that Comey had reason to believe the material could be used to harm the United States or benefit a foreign government, language reflecting elements of the federal law governing unauthorized disclosures of national defense information.
The two counts involve alleged transmission of national defense information and conspiracy to transmit such information.
However, the latest proceeding differs from a conventional federal indictment because prosecutors filed a criminal information without obtaining approval from a grand jury.
The distinction has become central to Comey’s legal challenge.
A criminal information is a charging document submitted directly by prosecutors rather than approved through a grand jury indictment. Federal felony prosecutions generally require a grand jury indictment unless the defendant waives that constitutional protection.
Comey has not waived indictment, and his attorneys argue that the government’s attempt to proceed through a criminal information is legally improper.
According to CBS News’ examination of the filing, the Justice Department submitted the document to preserve its ability to pursue charges before the 10-year statute of limitations expired.
The alleged disclosure occurred around Oct. 5, 2016, while prosecutors filed the criminal information exactly 10 years later.
A Justice Department spokesperson defended the procedure, describing the filing as a recognized method of preserving criminal allegations before a limitations deadline.
“The Department filed a waiverless criminal information to toll the statute of limitations as it relates to allegations concerning former FBI Director Comey,” the department said in a statement.
“Filing a criminal information to toll the statute of limitations is a widely recognized practice in federal court and has been approved by multiple Circuit Courts of Appeals. This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further.”
Comey’s attorneys dispute the government’s legal position and have requested dismissal of the case.
The former FBI director also publicly rejected the allegations Monday, accusing the administration of misusing federal law enforcement.
“It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice — one that we cannot become numb to,” Comey said in a video statement.
“Nothing’s changed with me. I’m still innocent.”
Comey’s attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, maintained that his client had not committed the alleged offenses and would continue challenging the prosecution.
The criminal information became public after Comey’s legal team sought to unseal the proceedings, which had remained confidential since early October.
According to Reuters’ reporting on the case, prosecutors allege that Comey conspired to provide sensitive information to a New York Times reporter concerning federal surveillance activities.
The alleged disclosure reportedly involved information connected to an October 2016 article about Yahoo’s assistance with a government email surveillance operation.
The filing does not establish that Comey personally transmitted the material. Prosecutors instead allege that he directed or participated in arrangements involving other individuals who communicated with the journalist.
Whether the government can establish that the information met the statutory definition of national defense information, that Comey knowingly authorized its disclosure and that the prosecution was initiated within applicable legal deadlines remains unresolved.
The new case adds to two previous federal criminal matters involving Comey since President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025.
In September 2025, federal prosecutors charged Comey with making false statements to Congress and obstructing a congressional proceeding in connection with his September 2020 testimony about FBI investigations and communications with journalists.
A federal judge dismissed that prosecution in November 2025 after determining that the prosecutor who obtained the indictment had been unlawfully appointed.
The Justice Department appealed the dismissal, leaving the dispute over the original charges unresolved.
Comey also faces a separate criminal prosecution in North Carolina concerning a May 2025 social media post depicting seashells arranged to form the numbers “8647.”
Federal authorities interpreted the image as a potential threat against Trump, the 47th president, because the number 86 can be used as slang for removing or eliminating someone.
Comey denied intending any threat and said he removed the image after learning that some people had interpreted it as advocating violence.
That prosecution remains pending.
The latest national defense information allegations therefore represent the administration’s third criminal case involving Comey, although the legal status of the proceedings differs.
The original congressional testimony case was dismissed and remains subject to appeal, the North Carolina case is ongoing, and the Washington prosecution faces an immediate procedural challenge because prosecutors have not secured a grand jury indictment.
The new filing also emerged on the same day a federal judge ruled that the Justice Department unlawfully dismissed Comey’s daughter, Maurene Comey, from her position as a federal prosecutor in Manhattan.
U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman determined that her July 2025 termination violated federal employment protections and ordered retroactive reinstatement and back pay for the period before she accepted another position.
The court did not determine whether her dismissal was motivated by her father’s disputes with the Trump administration.
The Justice Department has announced plans to appeal that decision.
James Comey’s relationship with Trump has been contentious since the president dismissed him as FBI director in May 2017.
Comey subsequently became a prominent public critic of Trump, while the president repeatedly accused him of misconduct during FBI investigations involving the 2016 presidential election and allegations of Russian interference.
The administration has maintained that prosecutions involving former government officials are based on alleged violations of federal law. Comey and his attorneys have argued that the repeated criminal proceedings against him constitute politically motivated retaliation.
Those competing allegations remain disputed.
The latest case will require federal courts to determine whether prosecutors can preserve potential felony charges through an information filed without a grand jury indictment and whether the government’s allegations can proceed under the applicable statute of limitations.
For now, Comey has denied wrongdoing, and the Justice Department has not obtained a conviction against him in any of the three criminal matters.

The Trump administration most recently charged Comey in April for a social media post, less than a year after he was initially charged in September 2025 for allegedly lying and obstructing a congressional investigation during testimony in 2020.
Comey, who was the FBI director when President Donald Trump first took office in January 2017, has been a frequent target of the president, who has publicly called for him to face criminal charges.
Monday’s complaint came just hours after a federal judge in New York ruled that the DOJ had unlawfully fired Comey’s daughter, Maurene Comey, last year as an assistant U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York.
Previous cases
Comey’s first case collapsed in November 2025, when a federal judge dismissed the indictment after ruling that Lindsey Halligan, the former White House aide Trump installed as interim U.S. attorney to bring charges, had been unlawfully appointed. Halligan had secured the indictment days before the statute of limitations was set to expire. The judge dismissed the case without prejudice, leaving the DOJ room to try again.
The April case, brought in the Eastern District of North Carolina, centers on a May 2025 Instagram post showing seashells on a beach arranged to spell out “86 47.” Prosecutors argue the post was a threat against Trump’s life, reading “86” as slang for killing someone and “47” as a reference to Trump as the 47th president. Comey, who deleted the post after backlash, has said he didn’t associate the term with violence. His later note “86” is commonly used in restaurants to mean getting rid of something.
That case is still pending. Comey has asked U.S. District Judge Louise Flanagan to dismiss it, arguing in part that the post is protected speech and that the prosecution is vindictive. Flanagan hasn’t ruled on the case. In September, she postponed Comey’s arraignment to January and pushed his trial into 2027.

sources.news_title: Justice Dept. charges James Comey, ex-FBI director, for a third time
Trump administration attempting to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey again - The Boston Globe
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is attempting to prosecute James Comey for what it calls a decade-old leak of classified information, an effort the former FBI director’s lawyers immediately dismissed as invalid and outside the time limit for when the Justice Department can file a case.
The allegations from the Justice Department came in documents unsealed Monday in federal court in Washington that shed light on a fight that has played out behind closed doors over the last month. It comes as prosecutors try to bring what would be the third criminal case against Comey, a longtime critic and foe of President Donald Trump, since the Republican returned to the White House last year.
“Well, they’re back — again,” Comey said in a video statement released after the documents dropped. “It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice – one that we cannot become numb to. Nothing’s changed with me; I’m still innocent, I’m still not afraid of these people — and I still believe in an independent federal judiciary.”
The Justice Department, for its part, said it had filed what’s known as a criminal information to extend the 10-year statute of limitations for bringing a case.
“Filing a criminal information to toll the statute of limitations is a widely recognized practice in federal court and has been approved by multiple Circuit Courts of Appeals. This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further,” a department spokesperson said.
Comey was the FBI director when Trump took office in 2017, having been appointed by then-President Barack Obama, a Democrat, and serving before that as a senior Justice Department official in President George W. Bush’s Republican administration.
But the relationship was strained from the start, including after Comey resisted a request by Trump at a private dinner to pledge his personal loyalty to the president -- an overture that so unnerved the FBI director that he documented it in a contemporaneous memorandum.
Trump fired Comey in May 2017 amid an FBI investigation into potential ties between Russia and Trump’s campaign. That inquiry, later taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller, found that while Russia interfered in the 2016 election and the Trump team welcomed the help, there was insufficient evidence to prove a criminal collaboration.

sources.news_title: DOJ charges ex-FBI Director James Comey in new case
sources.text:
Former FBI Director James Comey has been charged for the third time with federal crimes, according to a court filing unsealed Monday in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., at Comey's request.
Comey is accused in the new case with knowingly communicating information related to national defense to a person not entitled to receive it.
He is also charged with conspiring with others to violate the law against sharing such information.
The charging document, known as an information, says Comey, "through one or more co-conspirators," directed an unnamed individual "to disclose national defense information to a reporter for a national news publication."
Comey is seeking to dismiss the new case, according to a court filing by his lawyers, which says the information relates to the "alleged disclosure of classified information" to The New York Times on Oct. 5, 2016.
Comey's lawyers told a judge in that filing that the alleged disclosure "was investigated by two separate U.S. Attorneys over the past ten years. Both declined to prosecute."
Comey has been repeatedly targeted by the Department of Justice under the administration of President Donald Trump, who fired him as FBI director in 2017. Both men have been fierce critics of one another since then.
"For the third time in little more than one year, the Department of Justice has attempted to charge Mr. Comey with a federal crime. Mr. Comey steadfastly maintains his innocence," his attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement, according to The Associated Press.
The DOJ filed the information against Comey on Oct. 5 and asked a judge to seal it, citing the risk that an ongoing criminal investigation would be compromised by the charges becoming public. Judge Trevor McFadden granted that request that day.
Attorneys for Comey, whom the DOJ agreed should be notified of the information, filed a motion to dismiss the case on Oct. 9, arguing that the 10-year statute of limitations to file a grand jury indictment relating to events of Oct. 5, 2016, had expired.
Comey's lawyers accused the DOJ of filing "a faulty information under seal" in an effort to put the statute of limitations on hold.
The attorneys on Monday asked McFadden to unseal the information, and the judge agreed to do so.
Comey separately is currently seeking the dismissal of an indictment obtained by the DOJ in North Carolina federal court on charges of threatening Trump's life by posting a photo of seashells on a beach on social media. He previously successfully won dismissal of another indictment accusing him of falsely testifying to Congress.
The new criminal complaint came to light hours after a federal judge in New York ruled that the Department of Justice had unlawfully fired Comey's daughter, Maurene Comey, last year as an assistant U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York.
"Well, they're back — again," James Comey said in a video message on Substack addressing the new case.
"It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to," he said. "Nothing's changed with me. I'm still innocent. I'm still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary."
"And I'm still lucky to have an amazing family and an incredible group of lawyers that will stand up in court and fight the latest and whatever comes after this," Comey said. "The next couple of years are going to be hard for all of us. It's really important that we stand straight and keep the faith in America."
In the pending indictment in North Carolina, Comey in late April was charged with threatening Trump's life by posting on Instagram a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to form the numbers "86 47."
Prosecutors claim that the number "86" — which is often used in restaurants to indicate a menu item is no longer available — was code for suggesting someone kill Trump, who is the 47th U.S. president.
Comey has denied any wrongdoing in that case and is seeking to have the indictment tossed out by a judge.
Comey was first indicted in September 2025 by a federal grand jury in Virginia on charges of making a false statement and obstruction, in connection with testimony he gave before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Sept. 30, 2020.
Comey, in that testimony, denied authorizing another person at the FBI to serve as an anonymous source in news reports regarding an investigation of Hillary Clinton and her emails when she was the Democratic presidential nominee in 2016.
That first indictment was dismissed by a judge on Nov. 24, 2025, after the judge ruled that Lindsey Halligan, a then-interim U.S. attorney who obtained the indictments, had been invalidly appointed.
On the same day the judge tossed Comey's case for that reason, the same judge dismissed an unrelated indictment obtained by Halligan against New York Attorney General Letitia James, who had been accused of bank fraud and making false statements to a financial institution in connection with a home mortgage she obtained in 2020.
James, like Comey, has been a staunch critic of Trump, and a target of the president's ire.
